description: We are a team from Qaiwan International University (QIU), Sulaymaniyah, participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our goal is to develop an innovative health-monitoring software solution to support astronauts during space missions. Our interests include programming, artificial intelligence, data analysis, and software design. We welcome passionate students and creative thinkers who enjoy teamwork, solving real-world problems, and exploring space technology.
summary:
HUMAN.exe is an interactive health-monitoring prototype that makes daily astronaut assessments feel like a game instead of a clinical examination. During a short orbital-defense mission, the system uses on-device face and body tracking to observe movement, blinking, eye closure, head position, and gesture performance. After the mission, memory and Go/No-Go activities evaluate recall, focus, and reaction. Results are compared with the astronaut’s previous sessions to highlight changes that may need further attention.

The project was informed by three official NASA resources: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight, Risks of Human Spaceflight, and Ongoing Human Research Program Research. We used MediaPipe, OpenCV.js, Three.js, React, and JavaScript to create the observation system and 3D game. Camera processing happens locally, and no video or images are recorded. HUMAN.exe supports regular health observation and early screening but does not replace a qualified medical diagnosis.
details:
HUMAN.exe turns a routine astronaut health check into a short space mission. We built a browser-based prototype that combines a 3D orbital-defense game with movement, memory, and attention checks. Our goal is to make regular check-ins easier to fit into a crew’s day and give astronauts a way to notice changes in their own results over time.

How it works. During a two-minute mission, players defend a spacecraft. With camera controls enabled, they can aim with one hand, extend the other arm to fire, and raise both arms to activate a shield. These gestures are both game controls and a way to observe movement. An optional, separate 30-second face check measures visible signals such as blinking and eye closure. After the mission, players repeat a short pattern and respond to some signals while ignoring others. The app summarizes the results and compares them with earlier sessions completed under similar conditions. The reports support observation over time. A medical diagnosis requires a clinician.

How we built it. We used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and React for the web interface, and Three.js for the 3D game. MediaPipe models locate points on the face and body, OpenCV.js prepares camera frames, and JavaScript translates tracked movements into game commands. The prototype runs in a web browser. Camera features use a standard webcam, and keyboard controls are available.

What shaped the design. Three NASA resources informed our approach: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight, Risks of Human Spaceflight, and Ongoing HRP Research in Space. We considered privacy, limited space to move, and the reliability of webcam measurements. Players can play seated or standing and choose whether to enable camera observations. The device processes video locally without recording or uploading it. The app leaves measurements out of the report when lighting or tracking quality is too poor to use them.
